title: Rabi'a of Basra
hook: Rabi'a of Basra, who prayed to love Allah for Himself, not for heaven or fear of hell

segments.voice: Yesterday, ihsan, from the hadith of Jibril: to worship as though you see Him, and if you don't, He sees you. Your line was as though you see him. What did you do beautifully? Day two hundred ninety-five.

Why do you do the good things you do? Be honest. Some of it is love. Some of it is the reward: the thanks, the good feeling, the reputation. Some of it is fear of what happens if you don't. Most of us are a mix, and that's human. Now picture the streets of Basra, in southern Iraq, about a century after the Prophet. People tell a story about a woman walking through the city with a torch in one hand and a bucket of water in the other. Someone stops her and asks what she's doing. Today, her answer, and her name.
screen: `WHY DO YOU DO GOOD?` → `BASRA, A CENTURY LATER.` → `A TORCH AND A BUCKET.`

segments.voice: The woman is Rabi'a al-'Adawiyya, Rabi'a of Basra, who died around the year 800. In the story, she says: I want to set fire to paradise and pour water on the fires of hell, so that both veils are gone, and people worship God not out of hope for reward or fear of punishment, but for His own sake. It's a story people tell, not a sourced report. And here we need to be honest about the sources. Rabi'a left no writings. Most of what's told about her comes from biographies written centuries after she died, especially by the Persian poet Farid al-Din 'Attar, around four hundred years later. Tradition says she was born poor, was enslaved as a girl, and was freed because her master saw a light over her while she prayed at night. Historians can't confirm those details. What's consistent across the sources is the center of her teaching: love. Mahabbah. There's a prayer attributed to her, in the old Sufi books, that runs roughly like this: if I worship You out of fear of hell, then burn me in it; if I worship You hoping for paradise, then shut me out of it; but if I worship You for Your own sake, then don't hold back Your eternal beauty from me. The Qur'an speaks of people whom God loves and who love Him. Rabi'a took that and made it the whole point. She isn't saying heaven and hell don't matter; Muslims hold that they're real. She's asking what's underneath. Love for its own sake.
screen: `A STORY: FIRE ON PARADISE, WATER ON HELL.` · `NO WRITINGS; LATER BIOGRAPHIES.` · `MAHABBAH — LOVE.` · `FOR YOUR OWN SAKE.` · then, large: `LOVE FOR ITS OWN SAKE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one good thing with no reward. Sit, and breathe. Think of a small kindness you could do today that nobody will ever know was you. Paying for a stranger's coffee. Picking up litter on a street you'll never walk again. Praying for someone who doesn't know you exist. Choose it now. Notice the part of you that wants credit, and just smile at it. If you pray, you can ask to love for its own sake. The bell holds the time.
Rabi'a of Basra. The early woman saint of the Sufis, remembered for loving God for His own sake. Today's word.
Your line: love for its own sake. Today, do one good thing in secret, and don't tell anyone, not even later. Day two hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Sufis honor Rabi'a of Basra as one of the first to place pure love of God at the center of the path, and her attributed sayings are still taught in Sufi circles and recited in poetry.

what it means: an early woman saint who asked people to love God for Himself, not for reward or out of fear.
what a scholar hears: Rabi'a al-'Adawiyya (d. c. 801) left no texts; her image comes mostly from 'Attar's Tadhkirat al-Awliya, written centuries later.
